clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 70s presented with acute neurological symptoms including gait disturbance, left hemiparaesthesia, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Initial brain MRI showed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem and left caudate nucleus, suggestive of neuroinflammation. Physical examination did not reveal typical mucocutaneous manifestations of Behçet's disease, and a pathergy test was negative. CSF analysis was normal. However, the patient had a history of uveitis and retinitis pigmentosa in his 30s, and HLA analysis revealed homozygosity for the B51 alleles. Other autoimmune conditions, infections, and malignancies were ruled out by blood tests. Based on the acute brainstem lesion, MRI findings, and HLA-B51 positivity, neuro-Behçet's disease was suspected, and treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral corticosteroids and colchicine was initiated. The patient's symptoms gradually ameliorated, and follow-up MRI showed a reduction of the brain lesions, supporting the diagnosis.
